claim: Matriglycan [-GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-]n serves as a scaffold in many tissues for extracellular matrix proteins containing laminin-G domains including laminin, agrin, and perlecan.
source: Matriglycan [-GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-]n serves as a scaffold in many tissues for extracellular matrix proteins containing laminin-G domains including laminin, agrin, and perlecan.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about matriglycan function and is stated in the abstract.

claim: Like-acetyl-glucosaminyltransferase 1 (LARGE1) synthesizes and extends matriglycan on α-dystroglycan (α-DG) during skeletal muscle differentiation and regeneration.
source: Like-acetyl-glucosaminyltransferase 1 (LARGE1) synthesizes and extends matriglycan on α-dystroglycan (α-DG) during skeletal muscle differentiation and regeneration
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and is stated in the abstract.

claim: Protein O-Mannose Kinase (POMK) phosphorylates mannose of core M3 (GalNAc-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4-Man) preceding matriglycan synthesis.
source: Protein O-Mannose Kinase (POMK), which phosphorylates mannose of core M3 (GalNAc-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4-Man) preceding matriglycan synthesis
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about POMK function and is stated in the abstract.

claim: POMK is required for LARGE1-mediated generation of full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150 kDa).
source: Here, we show that Protein O-Mannose Kinase (POMK), which phosphorylates mannose of core M3 (GalNAc-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4-Man) preceding matriglycan synthesis, is required for LARGE1-mediated generation of full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150 kDa).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In the absence of Pomk gene expression in mouse skeletal muscle, LARGE1 synthesizes a very short matriglycan resulting in a ~ 90 kDa α-DG which binds laminin.
source: In the absence of Pomk gene expression in mouse skeletal muscle, LARGE1 synthesizes a very short matriglycan resulting in a ~ 90 kDa α-DG which binds laminin but cannot prevent eccentric contraction-induced force loss or muscle pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from POMK knockout mice shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: The ~90 kDa α-DG in POMK-deficient muscle cannot prevent eccentric contraction-induced force loss or muscle pathology.
source: In the absence of Pomk gene expression in mouse skeletal muscle, LARGE1 synthesizes a very short matriglycan resulting in a ~ 90 kDa α-DG which binds laminin but cannot prevent eccentric contraction-induced force loss or muscle pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle physiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: LARGE1 directly interacts with core M3.
source: Solution NMR spectroscopy studies demonstrate that LARGE1 directly interacts with core M3 and binds preferentially to the phosphorylated form.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR binding data shown in Figure 8.

claim: LARGE1 binds preferentially to the phosphorylated form of core M3.
source: Solution NMR spectroscopy studies demonstrate that LARGE1 directly interacts with core M3 and binds preferentially to the phosphorylated form.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR binding data showing different Kd values for phosphorylated vs unphosphorylated core M3 in Figure 8.

claim: Phosphorylation of core M3 by POMK enables LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan on α-DG.
source: Collectively, our study demonstrates that phosphorylation of core M3 by POMK enables LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan on α-DG, thereby preventing muscular dystrophy.
evidence: This is the central conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including biochemical, cellular, and NMR data.

claim: The heteropolysaccharide [-GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-]n is called matriglycan.
source: The heteropolysaccharide [-GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-]n (called matriglycan) is a scaffold for ECM proteins containing laminin-G (LG) domains (e.g. laminin, agrin, and perlecan) (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Hohenester, 2019; Michele et al., 2002; Ohtsubo and Marth, 2006)
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Matriglycan has the capacity to be tuned during skeletal muscle development and regeneration.
source: and has the remarkable capacity to be tuned during skeletal muscle development and regeneration (Goddeeris et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Over 18 genes are involved in the synthesis of the post-translational modification terminating in matriglycan.
source: Over 18 genes are involved in the synthesis of the post-translational modification terminating in matriglycan (Figure 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Defects in matriglycan synthesis cause dystroglycanopathies, i.e. congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies that can be accompanied by brain and eye defects.
source: and defects in this process cause dystroglycanopathies, i.e. congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies that can be accompanied by brain and eye defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by established clinical knowledge about dystroglycanopathies.

claim: Like-acetyl-glucosaminyltransferase 1 (LARGE1) synthesizes matriglycan on the cell-surface glycoprotein, α-dystroglycan (α-DG).
source: Like-acetyl-glucosaminyltransferase 1 (LARGE1) synthesizes matriglycan on the cell-surface glycoprotein, α-dystroglycan (α-DG) (Inamori et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Addition of matriglycan enables α-DG to serve as the predominant ECM receptor in skeletal muscle and brain.
source: Addition of matriglycan enables α-DG to serve as the predominant ECM receptor in skeletal muscle and brain (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Hohenester, 2019; Jae et al., 2013; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A single glucuronic acid-xylose disaccharide (GlcA-Xyl) repeat binds to laminin-α2 LG4 domain.
source: Crystal structure studies have shown that a single glucuronic acid-xylose disaccharide (GlcA-Xyl) repeat binds to laminin-α2 LG4 domain (Briggs et al., 2016; Hohenester et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structure studies.

claim: There is a direct correlation between the number of GlcA-Xyl repeats on α-DG and its binding capacity for ECM ligands.
source: and there is a direct correlation between the number of GlcA-Xyl repeats on α-DG and its binding capacity for ECM ligands (Goddeeris et al., 2013; Inamori et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During skeletal muscle differentiation, LARGE1 elongates matriglycan to its full length for normal skeletal muscle function.
source: During skeletal muscle differentiation, LARGE1 elongates matriglycan to its full length for normal skeletal muscle function (Goddeeris et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Complete loss-of-function mutations in the dystroglycanopathy genes abrogate synthesis of the post-translational modification terminating in matriglycan.
source: Complete loss-of-function mutations in the dystroglycanopathy genes abrogate synthesis of the post-translational modification terminating in matriglycan.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about dystroglycanopathies.

claim: Complete loss-of-function mutations in dystroglycanopathy genes cause Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS), which is lethal in utero or within a day or two of birth.
source: Such mutations preclude addition of matriglycan and, thereby, cause the most severe form of dystroglycanopathy, Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS), which is lethal in utero or within a day or two of birth (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Hohenester, 2019; Michele et al., 2002; Ohtsubo and Marth, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and established clinical knowledge.

claim: Protein O-Mannose Kinase (POMK) is a glycosylation-specific kinase that phosphorylates mannose of the core M3 trisaccharide (GalNAc-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4-Man) during synthesis of the O-mannose-linked polysaccharide ending in matriglycan.
source: Protein O-Mannose Kinase (POMK) is a glycosylation-specific kinase that phosphorylates mannose of the core M3 trisaccharide (GalNAc-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4-Man) during synthesis of the O-mannose-linked polysaccharide ending in matriglycan (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Hohenester, 2019; Jae et al., 2013; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Unlike with other dystroglycanopathy genes, there are patients with complete loss-of-function mutations in POMK who suffer from mild forms of dystroglycanopathy.
source: Interestingly, unlike with other dystroglycanopathy genes there are patients with complete loss-of-function mutations in POMK who suffer from mild forms of dystroglycanopathy (Di Costanzo et al., 2014; von Renesse et al., 2014), suggesting some expression of matriglycan without POMK.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical case reports.

claim: Phosphorylation of core M3 by POMK is not necessary for the LARGE1-mediated synthesis of a short, non-extended form of matriglycan on α-DG (~90 kDa) with reduced laminin-binding capacity.
source: Here, we have used a multidisciplinary approach to show that phosphorylation of core M3 by POMK is not necessary for the LARGE1-mediated synthesis of a short, non-extended form of matriglycan on α-DG (~90 kDa) with reduced laminin-binding capacity
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from POMK-deficient cells and mice.

claim: POMK activity is required for LARGE1 to generate full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150 kDa).
source: however, POMK activity is required for LARGE1 to generate full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150 kDa).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The non-extended matriglycan on ~90 kDa α-DG binds laminin and maintains specific force but cannot prevent eccentric contraction-induced force loss or skeletal muscle pathology.
source: In the absence of the phosphorylated core M3, the non-extended matriglycan on ~90 kDa α-DG binds laminin and maintains specific force but cannot prevent eccentric contraction-induced force loss or skeletal muscle pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle physiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Patient NH13-284 has a homozygous POMK (D204N) mutation.
source: To determine if matriglycan can be expressed in the absence of POMK function, and therefore better understand the role of POMK in matriglycan synthesis, we studied skeletal muscle from a patient (NH13-284) with a homozygous POMK (D204N) mutation (Figure 2A) and congenital muscular dystrophy (CMD) accompanied by structural brain malformations.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about a patient sample studied in the manuscript.

claim: Patient NH13-284 has congenital muscular dystrophy (CMD) accompanied by structural brain malformations.
source: we studied skeletal muscle from a patient (NH13-284) with a homozygous POMK (D204N) mutation (Figure 2A) and congenital muscular dystrophy (CMD) accompanied by structural brain malformations.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about a patient sample studied in the manuscript.

claim: D204 serves as the catalytic base in the phosphorylation reaction catalyzed by POMK.
source: D204 serves as the catalytic base in the phosphorylation reaction catalyzed by the kinase (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The D204N mutation is predicted to eliminate POMK activity.
source: and its mutation is predicted to eliminate POMK activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling and a citation to prior work.

claim: POMK activity from skin fibroblasts and skeletal muscle of patient NH13-284 (POMK D204N) was undetectable when compared to control fibroblasts and muscle, respectively.
source: POMK activity from skin fibroblasts and skeletal muscle of patient NH13-284 (POMK D204N) was undetectable when compared to control fibroblasts and muscle, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fibroblast LARGE1 activity of patient NH13-284 was similar to that of a control.
source: Fibroblast LARGE1 activity and skeletal muscle B4GAT1 activity of patient NH13-284 were similar to those of a control (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Skeletal muscle B4GAT1 activity of patient NH13-284 was similar to that of a control.
source: Fibroblast LARGE1 activity and skeletal muscle B4GAT1 activity of patient NH13-284 were similar to those of a control (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescence analyses of POMK D204N muscle demonstrated partial immunoreactivity to IIH6 (anti-matriglycan).
source: Immunofluorescence analyses of POMK D204N muscle demonstrated partial immunoreactivity to IIH6 (anti-matriglycan), while the transmembrane subunit of DG, β-DG, was expressed normally in POMK D204N muscle (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The transmembrane subunit of DG, β-DG, was expressed normally in POMK D204N muscle.
source: while the transmembrane subunit of DG, β-DG, was expressed normally in POMK D204N muscle (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Flow cytometry using IIH6 demonstrated partial immunoreactivity in POMK D204N fibroblasts.
source: Flow cytometry using IIH6 also demonstrated partial immunoreactivity in POMK D204N fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Control human skeletal muscle showed the typical broad band of α-DG laminin binding centered at ~150 kDa range.
source: Control human skeletal muscle showed the typical broad band of α-DG laminin binding centered at ~150 kDa range; in contrast, laminin binding at ~90 to 100 kDa range with reduced intensity was observed in POMK D204N skeletal muscle (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Laminin binding at ~90 to 100 kDa range with reduced intensity was observed in POMK D204N skeletal muscle.
source: in contrast, laminin binding at ~90 to 100 kDa range with reduced intensity was observed in POMK D204N skeletal muscle (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Histologic analyses of MckCre; Pax7Cre; PomkLoxP/LoxP (M-POMK KO) quadriceps muscles revealed hallmarks of a mild muscular dystrophy.
source: Histologic analyses of MckCre; Pax7Cre; PomkLoxP/LoxP (M-POMK KO) quadriceps muscles revealed hallmarks of a mild muscular dystrophy (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Quadriceps muscle extracts of MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP mice showed reduced POMK activity compared to PomkLoxP/LoxP muscle.
source: Quadriceps muscle extracts of MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP mice showed reduced POMK activity compared to PomkLoxP/LoxP muscle but had similar levels of LARGE1 activity (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Quadriceps muscle extracts of MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP mice had similar levels of LARGE1 activity compared to PomkLoxP/LoxP muscle.
source: Quadriceps muscle extracts of MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP mice showed reduced POMK activity compared to PomkLoxP/LoxP muscle but had similar levels of LARGE1 activity (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: M-POMK KO mice showed reductions in 2-limb grip strength compared to littermate control PomkLoxP/LoxP mice.
source: M-POMK KO mice also showed reductions in 2-limb grip strength and body weight, and elevations in post-exercise creatine kinase (CK) levels compared to littermate control PomkLoxP/LoxP mice (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: M-POMK KO mice showed reductions in body weight compared to littermate control PomkLoxP/LoxP mice.
source: M-POMK KO mice also showed reductions in 2-limb grip strength and body weight, and elevations in post-exercise creatine kinase (CK) levels compared to littermate control PomkLoxP/LoxP mice (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: M-POMK KO mice showed elevations in post-exercise creatine kinase (CK) levels compared to littermate control PomkLoxP/LoxP mice.
source: M-POMK KO mice also showed reductions in 2-limb grip strength and body weight, and elevations in post-exercise creatine kinase (CK) levels compared to littermate control PomkLoxP/LoxP mice (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by creatine kinase data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of M-POMK KO muscle showed that β-DG is expressed at the skeletal muscle sarcolemma.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of M-POMK KO muscle showed that β-DG is expressed at the skeletal muscle sarcolemma (Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IIH6 immunoreactivity persisted in M-POMK KO muscle, but at a reduced intensity.
source: however, like patient NH13-284 IIH6 immunoreactivity persisted in M-POMK KO muscle, but at a reduced intensity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EDL muscle mass was reduced in M-POMK KO mice compared to control mice.
source: EDL muscle mass and cross-sectional area (CSA) were reduced in M-POMK KO mice compared to control mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle mass data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EDL cross-sectional area (CSA) was reduced in M-POMK KO mice compared to control mice.
source: EDL muscle mass and cross-sectional area (CSA) were reduced in M-POMK KO mice compared to control mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CSA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M-POMK KO EDL absolute isometric tetanic force production was significantly lower than that of controls.
source: Additionally, M-POMK KO EDL absolute isometric tetanic force production was significantly lower than that of controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by force production data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When normalized to muscle CSA, force production in M-POMK KO EDL was comparable to control values.
source: However, when normalized to muscle CSA, force production was comparable to control values (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by specific force data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: EDL muscles of M-POMK KO mice demonstrated greater force deficits after five and eight lengthening contractions compared to Control EDL.
source: EDL muscles of M-POMK KO mice demonstrated greater force deficits after five and eight lengthening contractions (LC) and recovered to a lower level after 45 min compared to Control EDL (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by eccentric contraction data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: EDL muscles of M-POMK KO mice recovered to a lower level after 45 min compared to Control EDL.
source: EDL muscles of M-POMK KO mice demonstrated greater force deficits after five and eight lengthening contractions (LC) and recovered to a lower level after 45 min compared to Control EDL (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by eccentric contraction recovery data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Control and M-POMK KO muscle showed a typical, lower molecular weight (MW) α-DG with anti-core DG antibody.
source: Biochemical analysis of control and M-POMK KO muscle showed a typical, lower molecular weight (MW) α-DG with anti-core DG antibody (Figure 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: On laminin overlay, laminin binding at 90–100 kDa was observed in M-POMK KO muscle.
source: however, on laminin overlay, we observed laminin binding at 90–100 kDa (Figure 5B), similar to POMK D204N skeletal muscle (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IIH6 showed binding at 90–100 kDa in M-POMK KO muscle.
source: IIH6 also showed binding at 90–100 kDa (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Solid-phase binding analyses of M-POMK KO and MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP skeletal muscle demonstrated a reduced binding capacity (relative Bmax) for laminin-111 compared to control muscle.
source: Solid-phase binding analyses of M-POMK KO and MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP skeletal muscle demonstrated a reduced binding capacity (relative Bmax) for laminin-111 compared to control muscle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), but higher than that of Largemyd muscle, which lacks matriglycan due to a deletion in Large.
evidence: This claim is supported by solid-phase binding data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: M-POMK KO skeletal muscle has higher laminin-111 binding capacity than Largemyd muscle, which lacks matriglycan due to a deletion in Large.
source: Solid-phase binding analyses of M-POMK KO and MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP skeletal muscle demonstrated a reduced binding capacity (relative Bmax) for laminin-111 compared to control muscle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), but higher than that of Largemyd muscle, which lacks matriglycan due to a deletion in Large.
evidence: This claim is supported by solid-phase binding data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Laminin overlay and solid-phase analysis showed a reduction in laminin binding from M-POMK KO and MckCre; PomkLoxP/LoxP muscles after dual exoglycosidase digestion.
source: Laminin overlay and solid-phase analysis showed a reduction in laminin binding from these muscles after dual exoglycosidase digestion (Figure 5D and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by exoglycosidase digestion data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: POMK KO HAP1 cells have undetectable levels of POMK activity and expression.
source: To study the role of POMK further, we used human POMK KO HAP1 cells, which have undetectable levels of POMK activity and expression (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity and expression data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, and a citation to prior work.

claim: A mass spectrometry (MS)-based glycomic analysis of O-glycans carried by recombinantly-expressed DG mucin-like domain indicated the near complete absence of an MS peak at m/z 873.5 corresponding to phosphorylated core M3 O-glycan in POMK KO HAP1 cells.
source: A mass spectrometry (MS)-based glycomic analysis of O-glycans carried by recombinantly-expressed DG mucin-like domain indicated the near complete absence of an MS peak at m/z 873.5 corresponding to phosphorylated core M3 O-glycan (Figure 6D and E; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), consistent with an undetectable level of POMK activity in POMK KO HAP1 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Compared to WT HAP1 cells, immunoblots of POMK KO HAP1 cells showed a reduction in IIH6 immunoreactivity.
source: Compared to WT HAP1 cells, immunoblots of POMK KO HAP1 cells showed a reduction in IIH6 immunoreactivity, a decrease in MW of core α-DG, and the presence of laminin binding at ~90 kDa on laminin overlay (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Compared to WT HAP1 cells, immunoblots of POMK KO HAP1 cells showed a decrease in MW of core α-DG.
source: Compared to WT HAP1 cells, immunoblots of POMK KO HAP1 cells showed a reduction in IIH6 immunoreactivity, a decrease in MW of core α-DG, and the presence of laminin binding at ~90 kDa on laminin overlay (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: POMK KO HAP1 cells showed the presence of laminin binding at ~90 kDa on laminin overlay.
source: Compared to WT HAP1 cells, immunoblots of POMK KO HAP1 cells showed a reduction in IIH6 immunoreactivity, a decrease in MW of core α-DG, and the presence of laminin binding at ~90 kDa on laminin overlay (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Laminin binding on overlay was rescued only after adenoviral transduction with wild-type (WT) POMK (POMK WT), but not with POMK containing D204N (POMK D204N) or D204A (POMK D204A) mutations.
source: Laminin binding on overlay was rescued only after adenoviral transduction with wild-type (WT) POMK (POMK WT), but not with POMK containing D204N (POMK D204N) or D204A (POMK D204A) mutations (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: POMK D204N lacked POMK activity in vitro but showed normal B4GAT1, B3GALNT2, and LARGE1 activity.
source: POMK D204N also lacked POMK activity in vitro but showed normal B4GAT1, B3GALNT2, and LARGE1 activity, thus confirming the pathogenicity of the D204N mutation (Figure 6A and B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: POMK/LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated the absence of the laminin binding at 90 kDa.
source: POMK/LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated the absence of the laminin binding at 90 kDa (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that LARGE1 is required for the synthesis of the matriglycan responsible for laminin binding at 90 kDa.
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: LARGE1 is required for the synthesis of the matriglycan responsible for laminin binding at 90 kDa.
source: POMK/LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated the absence of the laminin binding at 90 kDa (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that LARGE1 is required for the synthesis of the matriglycan responsible for laminin binding at 90 kDa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing loss of laminin binding in POMK/LARGE1 double knockout cells.

claim: POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated a complete absence of laminin binding.
source: Moreover, POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated a complete absence of laminin binding (Figure 7A) and IIH6 immunoreactivity at 90 kDa (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that α-DG is the glycoprotein that binds laminin in the absence of POMK.
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated a complete absence of IIH6 immunoreactivity at 90 kDa.
source: Moreover, POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated a complete absence of laminin binding (Figure 7A) and IIH6 immunoreactivity at 90 kDa (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that α-DG is the glycoprotein that binds laminin in the absence of POMK.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: α-DG is the glycoprotein that binds laminin in the absence of POMK.
source: Moreover, POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells demonstrated a complete absence of laminin binding (Figure 7A) and IIH6 immunoreactivity at 90 kDa (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that α-DG is the glycoprotein that binds laminin in the absence of POMK.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing loss of laminin binding in POMK/DAG1 double knockout cells.

claim: Bmax of α-DG(POMK) for laminin-111 was reduced compared to wild-type α-DG (α-DG(WT)) but was greater than that of α-DG from LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells.
source: Bmax of α-DG(POMK) for laminin-111 was reduced compared to wild-type α-DG (α-DG(WT)) but was greater than that of α-DG from LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by solid-phase binding data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells showed a reduction in Bmax compared to POMK KO HAP1 cells, but similar to the low levels observed in LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells.
source: POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells showed a reduction in Bmax compared to POMK KO HAP1 cells, but similar to the low levels observed in LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by solid-phase binding data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A short, non-extended form of matriglycan is synthesized on α-DG(POMK), and this short form has a lower binding capacity for laminin-111.
source: These data indicate that a short, non-extended form of matriglycan is synthesized on α-DG(POMK), and this short form has a lower binding capacity for laminin-111, thus exhibiting a reduced level of α-DG receptor function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding capacity data and molecular weight observations.

claim: Overexpression of ISPD in POMK KO HAP1 cells increases the amount of matriglycan responsible for laminin binding at 90 kDa.
source: Overexpression in POMK KO HAP1 cells of ISPD, which synthesizes the substrate (CDP-ribitol) of FKTN (Figure 1), increases the amount of matriglycan (without changing its migration on SDS-PAGE) responsible for laminin binding at 90 kDa (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B and C; Willer et al., 2012; Gerin et al., 2016; Riemersma et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior work.

claim: HAP1 cells lacking both POMK and ISPD do not express matriglycan.
source: HAP1 cells lacking both POMK and ISPD do not express matriglycan, and adenoviral transduction of these cells with ISPD restores the 90 kDa laminin binding (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Adenoviral transduction of POMK/ISPD KO HAP1 cells with ISPD restores the 90 kDa laminin binding.
source: HAP1 cells lacking both POMK and ISPD do not express matriglycan, and adenoviral transduction of these cells with ISPD restores the 90 kDa laminin binding (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: FKTN overexpression in POMK KO HAP1 cells increased the 90 kDa laminin binding.
source: FKTN overexpression in POMK KO HAP1 cells also increased the 90 kDa laminin binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Synthesis of the non-extended form of matriglycan requires CDP-ribitol.
source: These experiments collectively support a requirement for CDP-ribitol for synthesis of the non-extended form of matriglycan.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that ISPD and FKTN overexpression increase matriglycan in POMK KO cells.

claim: Synthesis of the non-extended form of matriglycan requires the N-terminal domain of α-DG (DGN).
source: This synthesis also requires the N-terminal domain of α-DG (DGN) (Hara et al., 2011a; Kanagawa et al., 2004), as a DG mutant lacking the DGN (DGE) expressed in POMK/DAG1 KO HAP1 cells did not show laminin binding at 90 kDa (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 and citations to prior work.

claim: Synthesis of the non-extended matriglycan in HAP1 cells requires threonine-317 of the mucin-like domain of α-DG.
source: Similar experiments also indicated that synthesis of the non-extended matriglycan in HAP1 cells requires threonine-317 of the mucin-like domain of α-DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Overexpression of LARGE1 can rescue the defect in matriglycan synthesis in distinct forms of CMD as well as in LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells by generating very high molecular weight matriglycan.
source: Overexpression of LARGE1 can rescue the defect in matriglycan synthesis in distinct forms of CMD as well as in LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells by generating very high molecular weight matriglycan (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A; Barresi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5A and a citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of LARGE1 in POMK or POMK/LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells did not produce very high molecular weight matriglycan.
source: However, overexpression of LARGE1 in POMK or POMK/LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells did not produce very high molecular weight matriglycan (Figure 7D and E; Figure 7—figure supplement 5B, C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Only the rescue of POMK/LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells with POMK enabled LARGE1 to synthesize high molecular weight matriglycan.
source: Only the rescue of POMK/LARGE1 KO HAP1 cells with POMK enabled LARGE1 to synthesize high molecular weight matriglycan (Figure 7E; Figure 7—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: LARGE1 requires phosphorylated core M3 to extend matriglycan on α-DG to its mature and high molecular weight forms.
source: These findings indicate that LARGE1 requires phosphorylated core M3 to extend matriglycan on α-DG to its mature and high molecular weight forms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that LARGE1 overexpression cannot rescue matriglycan synthesis in POMK KO cells.

claim: The unphosphorylated core M3 binds to POMK with high affinity.
source: We previously showed that the unphosphorylated core M3 binds to POMK with high affinity (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The phosphorylated core M3 of GGMp-MU binds to POMK with a dissociation constant of >500 µM.
source: By fitting the intensity changes of the Man H1 peak as a function of POMK concentration, we obtained a dissociation constant of >500 µM (Figure 8C; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR binding data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Compared to the unphosphorylated core M3 of GGM-MU, the phosphorylated core M3 of GGMp-MU binds to POMK with a much weaker affinity.
source: These results indicate that, compared to the unphosphorylated core M3 of GGM-MU, the phosphorylated core M3 of GGMp-MU binds to POMK with a much weaker affinity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the NMR binding data comparing Kd values.

claim: LARGE1 binds with greater affinity to GGMp-MU compared to GGM-MU (Kd = 11.5 ± 1.2 µM for GGMp-MU compared to Kd >90 µM for GGM-MU).
source: Our results showed that LARGE1 binds with greater affinity to GGMp-MU compared to GGM-MU (Kd = 11.5 ± 1.2 µM for GGMp-MU compared to Kd >90 µM for GGM-MU) (Figure 8A, B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR binding data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The core M3 phosphate increases the binding affinity of LARGE1 for core M3.
source: This indicates that the core M3 phosphate increases the binding affinity of LARGE1 for core M3 and could explain the ability of LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan in the presence of POMK.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the NMR binding data showing differential affinity.

claim: The short form of matriglycan is able to bind to laminin with high affinity and thus enables α-DG(POMK) to function as an ECM receptor.
source: Our study shows that the short form of matriglycan is able to bind to laminin with high affinity and thus enables α-DG(POMK) to function as an ECM receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by laminin binding data from POMK-deficient cells and tissues.

claim: The short, non-extended form of matriglycan likely contains few Xyl-GlcA repeats.
source: Given the very small increase in apparent MW in α-DG(POMK) compared to α-DG from cells and muscle lacking LARGE1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A; Figure 8—figure supplement 3A), the short, non-extended form of matriglycan likely contains few Xyl-GlcA repeats.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the molecular weight data comparing different conditions.

claim: Only a single Xyl-GlcA repeat is needed for laminin binding.
source: However, it can still bind laminin since only a single Xyl-GlcA repeat is needed for laminin binding (Briggs et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: The short matriglycan likely attenuates muscular dystrophy in patient NH13-284 with a complete loss-of-function mutation in POMK, preventing the severe WWS phenotype.
source: This short matriglycan likely attenuates muscular dystrophy in patient NH13-284 with a complete loss-of-function mutation in POMK, preventing the severe WWS phenotype that is observed in the complete absence of the other known dystroglycanopathy genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the clinical observation that POMK patients have milder disease than other dystroglycanopathy patients.

claim: Muscle-specific POMK KO mice express the short, non-extended form of matriglycan on ~90 kDa α-DG and develop a mild muscular dystrophy phenotype.
source: Muscle-specific POMK KO mice express the short, non-extended form of matriglycan on ~90 kDa α-DG and develop a mild muscular dystrophy phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from M-POMK KO mice shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: The short matriglycan expressed in the absence of POMK can maintain specific force but cannot prevent eccentric contraction-induced force loss or skeletal muscle pathology.
source: Muscle physiology studies demonstrate that the short matriglycan expressed in the absence of POMK can maintain specific force but cannot prevent eccentric contraction-induced force loss or skeletal muscle pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle physiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Missense mutations in FKRP that cause LGMD2I show reduced expression of matriglycan and exhibit a milder muscular dystrophy.
source: Interestingly, missense mutations in FKRP that cause LGMD2I also show reduced expression of matriglycan (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015) and exhibit a milder muscular dystrophy.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and established clinical knowledge.

claim: M-POMK KO mice are an excellent model of milder forms of dystroglycanopathy in which short matriglycan is expressed.
source: Thus, M-POMK KO mice are an excellent model of milder forms of dystroglycanopathy in which short matriglycan is expressed and will be useful for future studies of these forms of dystroglycanopathy.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the characterization of the M-POMK KO mouse model.

claim: α-DG is composed of three domains: the DGN, a central mucin-like domain, and a C-terminus.
source: α-DG is composed of three domains: the DGN, which undergoes cleavage at arginine-312 by a furin-like convertase during α-DG post-translational processing, a central mucin-like domain, and a C-terminus (Kanagawa et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work describing α-DG structure.

claim: The DGN undergoes cleavage at arginine-312 by a furin-like convertase during α-DG post-translational processing.
source: the DGN, which undergoes cleavage at arginine-312 by a furin-like convertase during α-DG post-translational processing
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The synthesis of the short, non-extended form of matriglycan occurs on threonine-317 of the mucin-like domain.
source: Biochemical studies using various POMK KO HAP1 cell lines demonstrated that the synthesis of the short, non-extended form of matriglycan occurs on threonine-317 of the mucin-like domain and, like full-length matriglycan, requires LARGE1, DGN, and CDP-ribitol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HAP1 cell lines.

claim: The synthesis of the short, non-extended form of matriglycan requires LARGE1, DGN, and CDP-ribitol.
source: Biochemical studies using various POMK KO HAP1 cell lines demonstrated that the synthesis of the short, non-extended form of matriglycan occurs on threonine-317 of the mucin-like domain and, like full-length matriglycan, requires LARGE1, DGN, and CDP-ribitol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HAP1 cell lines.

claim: The binding of LARGE1 to the DGN is essential for the synthesis of full-length matriglycan on α-DG.
source: As the binding of LARGE1 to the DGN is essential for the synthesis of full-length matriglycan on α-DG (Kanagawa et al., 2004; Hara et al., 2011a), it is required for synthesis of the short form of matriglycan as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The binding of LARGE1 to the DGN is required for synthesis of the short form of matriglycan.
source: As the binding of LARGE1 to the DGN is essential for the synthesis of full-length matriglycan on α-DG (Kanagawa et al., 2004; Hara et al., 2011a), it is required for synthesis of the short form of matriglycan as well.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the requirement for DGN in both full-length and short matriglycan synthesis.

claim: The phosphorylated core M3 could serve to recruit DGN-bound LARGE1 to the proper residue during the initiation of full-length matriglycan synthesis.
source: The phosphorylated core M3, could, therefore serve to recruit DGN-bound LARGE1 to the proper residue during the initiation of full-length matriglycan synthesis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the binding data.

claim: In the absence of the mannose phosphate, the DGN-bound LARGE1 may instead act only upon the matriglycan acceptor added to threonine-317, the threonine nearest to the DGN.
source: In the absence of the mannose phosphate, the DGN-bound LARGE1 may instead act only upon the matriglycan acceptor added to threonine-317, the threonine nearest to the DGN.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Synthesis of full-length matriglycan may proceed through a complex of DGN, LARGE1, and phosphorylated core M3.
source: Synthesis of full-length matriglycan may, therefore, proceed through a complex of DGN, LARGE1, and phosphorylated core M3.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the binding and functional data.

claim: The phosphorylated core M3 may serve to anchor LARGE1 to α-DG during matriglycan elongation.
source: The phosphorylated core M3 may also serve to anchor LARGE1 to α-DG during matriglycan elongation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the binding data.

claim: In the absence of POMK, the binding of LARGE1 to the DGN and the unphosphorylated core M3 may only be sufficient for synthesis of a short form of matriglycan.
source: In the absence of POMK, the binding of LARGE1 to the DGN and the unphosphorylated core M3 may only be sufficient for synthesis of a short form of matriglycan.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: LARGE1 requires DGN to synthesize the short, non-extended form of matriglycan but needs both the DGN and the phosphorylated core M3 to generate full-length matriglycan on α-DG.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that LARGE1 requires DGN to synthesize the short, non-extended form of matriglycan but needs both the DGN and the phosphorylated core M3 to generate full-length matriglycan on α-DG.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: POMK is required for the synthesis of full-length and high-molecular weight forms of matriglycan.
source: Our study demonstrates that POMK is required for the synthesis of full-length and high-molecular weight forms of matriglycan (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: In the absence of POMK, LARGE1 generates a short, non-extended form of matriglycan.
source: In the absence of POMK, LARGE1 generates a short, non-extended form of matriglycan (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.
